l: the victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: The victory took place in the Olympic games and is dated to 476 B.C. It brought honour to Asopichos's father and to the Minyai's home.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: The ode was composed for Asopichos's victory and was probably sung by a chorus of boys at Orchomenos. It was most likely performed in the temple of the three Graces.

l: Graces, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: The Graces are invoked as the renowned queens of Orchomenos and guardians of the Minyai's ancient race. They are said to give men pleasant things, wisdom, beauty, and fame, and to share authority over heavenly feasts and dances beside Pythian Apollo.

l: the Minyai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: The Minyai are identified with an ancient race whose home is Orchomenos. Their home is proclaimed the winner in the Olympic games through Asopichos.

l: Aglaia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: Aglaia is addressed as one of the Graces and as a daughter of the mightiest of the gods. The ode credits her with bringing about the Minyai's Olympic victory and asks her to look upon the triumphal company.

l: Euphrosyne, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: Euphrosyne is addressed as a Grace, a daughter of the mightiest of the gods, and a lover of song. She is asked to listen and to look upon the triumphal company.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: The Olympic games are where Asopichos won the boys' short foot-race. In their famous contests at Pisa's valley, he crowned his boyish hair with garlands.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, THE PYTHIAN ODES.
s: The unit is titled “THE PYTHIAN ODES.” No further content or details are provided.

l: The Pythian Odes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, THE PYTHIAN ODES.
s: The Pythian Odes is identified as the title of this unit. No additional information about it is given.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: The unit is Pindar’s victory ode for Hieron of Aitna, celebrating his chariot-race victory at the Pythian Games. It praises Aitna city, founded by Hieron under Dorian laws, and recalls the Syracusans’ victories over the Carthaginians at Himera and the Etruscans before Cumae. The poem invokes Zeus, Apollo, the Muses, and the Lyre, and describes Typhon imprisoned beneath Mount Etna. It also counsels Hieron to govern truthfully, preserve his reputation, and seek lasting happiness and glory.

l: Hieron of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Hieron is celebrated for winning the chariot-race at the Pythian Games. He is praised as the captain of the Syracusans before Cumae, the founder of Aitna city, and a ruler urged to govern truthfully and honor his people.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Pindar speaks as the singer who praises Hieron, his victories, and his city. He compares his own praise to throwing a bronze-tipped javelin beyond his rivals and asks the Muse to honor the house of Deinomenes.

l: Aitna, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Aitna is described as the mountain beneath which Typhon lies imprisoned and from which fire and lava emerge. The ode asks Zeus to favor the mountain and its fruitful land.

l: Aitna city, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Aitna city was founded by Hieron near the mountain and was ennobled when its name was proclaimed after Hieron’s chariot victory. It was founded with freedom under laws of Dorian, Hyllic pattern.

l: chariot-race victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Hieron’s chariot-race victory is the central occasion of the ode. The victory was won at the Pythian Games, where the herald proclaimed the name of Aitna.

l: Pythian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: At the Pythian Games, Hieron won the chariot-race. The herald proclaimed Aitna’s name aloud in connection with the victory.

l: battle of Himera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: In the battle of Himera, the Syracusans under Hieron defeated the Carthaginians. The victory is presented as a defense of the sons of Deinomenes and as a deed worthy of song.

l: battle before Cumae, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Before Cumae, Hieron and the Syracusans defeated the Etruscans in a great sea-fight. Their victory destroyed enemy ships and helped deliver Hellas from the bondage of the oppressor.

l: Syracusans, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: The Syracusans under Hieron defeated the Carthaginians at Himera and the Etruscans before Cumae. Their victories are likened to the Hellenes’ wars against the barbarians of the East.

l: Hellenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: The Hellenes are described as having fought barbarians in the East. The Syracusans’ victories against enemies in the South and West are presented as part of the same broader struggle.

l: Lyre, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: The golden Lyre is called the common treasure of Apollo and the violet-tressed Muses. Its music makes the dancer obey, guides singers, quenches immortal lightning, lulls Zeus’s eagle, and brings rest even to Ares.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Zeus is invoked as the defender of Mount Etna and as the one with whom the outcomes of things rest. The speaker asks him to favor the mountain, grant good fortune to Aitna, and silence the Phoenician and Tuscan war-cry.

l: Typhon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Typhon is described as a foe of the gods with a hundred heads, bred in the Kilikian cave. He lies bound beneath Etna and the cliffs beyond Cumae, producing fire, smoke, and lava from beneath the mountain.

l: Cumae, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Cumae is the place before which the Syracusans defeated the Etruscans in a sea-fight. Its surrounding cliffs are also said to lie heavily on the imprisoned Typhon.

l: Philoktetes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Philoktetes is used as an example for Hieron, who is said to have gone to war in a comparable way. Although Philoktetes suffered from an ulcerous wound, he was fetched from Lemnos, sacked Priam’s city, and ended the Danaoi’s labors.

l: Deinomenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: The house and sons of Deinomenes are honored in the ode. Their victories at Himera are said to have earned song, and the speaker asks the Muse to sing for their house.

l: music and poetry, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Music and poetry are presented as divine gifts that soothe gods, guide dancers and singers, and preserve the memory of the living after death. The speaker says that singers and chroniclers reveal the lives of the dead through lasting report.

l: Freedom, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: Aitna city is said to have been founded with god-built freedom under laws of Hyllic pattern. Hieron’s victory before Cumae is also associated with delivering Hellas from the bondage of an oppressor.

l: glory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, I.
s: The ode urges Hieron to seek good report through truthful speech, generous action, and proper rule. It teaches that loving-kindness, like that of Craesus, can remain memorable, while cruelty, like that of Phalaris, is remembered with hatred; happiness is called the chief prize and glory the next.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: This unit consists of four footnotes. One identifies Typhon, another records the reading “erion,” and a third refers to Plataea. The fourth explains that it is better to be envied than pitied.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The unit presents Pindar's ode for Hieron of Syracuse, celebrating his victory in the four-horse chariot-race and his protective action toward the Epizephyrian Lokrians against Anaxilaos. It praises Syracuse, Hieron's military valor, wealth, wisdom, and generosity, while using the story of Ixion's crimes and punishment to teach that favors should be repaid and that one must judge one's powers and circumstances rightly. The closing section condemns flattery, slander, envy, and crooked conduct, and commends sincerity and direct speech under every form of government.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Pindar presents himself as sending the ode from bright Thebes across the sea to Syracuse. He praises Hieron's victory, protection of the Lokrians, military valor, wealth, wisdom, and directness, while condemning bitter speech, flattery, slander, and crooked conduct.

l: Hieron of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Hieron wins the four-horse chariot-race and crowns Ortygia with splendid renown. He is praised as a powerful ruler with wealth, wisdom, military valor, generous character, and the strength to protect the western Lokrians from the troubles of war.

l: Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Syracuse is addressed as a great city, precinct of warrior Ares, and divine nursing-place of iron-armed men and horses. Pindar sends the ode there from Thebes.

l: Anaxilaos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Anaxilaos, tyrant of Rhegium and Messana, was deterred by Hieron's threats from attacking the Epizephyrian Lokrians.

l: Lokrians, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The Epizephyrian Lokrians were protected by Hieron from the troubles of war and from Anaxilaos's threatened attack. Their maiden daughter is said to sing of her deliverance before the house-door.

l: chariot-race victory of Hieron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Hieron's victory in the four-horse chariot-race is the central occasion celebrated by the ode. His success brings splendid crowns and renown to Ortygia and Syracuse.

l: protective act toward the Lokrians, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Hieron's protective act consisted in deterring Anaxilaos from attacking the Epizephyrian Lokrians. The ode treats the act as worthy of gratitude and praise.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The ode is sent from Pindar's bright Thebes to Syracuse like merchandise across the sea. It celebrates Hieron's chariot victory and protection of the Lokrians, and later commends sincerity while condemning flattery, slander, envy, and deceit.

l: Ixion, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Ixion is punished for shedding the blood of his kindred and attempting Hera, the wife of Zeus. After enjoying prosperity among the Kronidai, he lusts after Hera, lies with a cloud made in her form, and becomes an example proclaiming that service should be repaid with a fair reward.

l: Hera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Hera is the wife of Zeus whom Ixion attempts to approach. Zeus creates a cloud in her likeness as a snare for Ixion.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Zeus is the husband of Hera and makes the cloud-phantom in her form to trap Ixion. He is also described as a god who brings down human pride and gives glory to others.

l: Ixion's winged wheel, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Ixion writhes on a winged, four-spoked wheel as punishment. From it he proclaims to humanity that anyone who receives service should repay it with a fair reward.

l: four-horse car, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The four-horse car carries Hieron to victory in the earth-shaking race. Its horses are yoked with polished, bridle-guided equipment, while Artemis and Hermes are invoked in connection with the race.

l: war, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: War and military valor are presented as grounds for Hieron's boundless renown. He is praised for victories in battles fought both with horsemen and on foot, while the counsels of his older years provide further cause for praise.

l: wealth and wisdom, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The ode declares that riches are most valuable when joined with the gift of wisdom. Hieron is said to possess this combination and to rule as a sovereign over many streets and much people.

l: sincerity and direct speech, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Sincerity and direct speech are commended as the proper qualities of a good citizen. Direct speech is said to be best under despotism, rule by the multitude, or rule by the wisest, and the speaker wishes to dwell among the good and win their love.

l: flattery, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Flattery is condemned as fawning and deceptive conduct. The ode contrasts the childish appeal of a fawning ape with the true inward character associated with Rhadamanthos's good fortune.

l: treacherous speech and slander, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Slander is described as a powerful evil that harms both the person slandered and the listener. Its secret whispers are compared to foxes, and those who use such crooked speech are rejected in favor of directness.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The ode celebrates Hieron of Syracuse and the Pythian victory won by his horse Pherenikos at Kirrha. It recounts how Apollo rescued Asklepios from the burning corpse of Koronis and had him trained by Cheiron as a healer, but Zeus later killed Asklepios for restoring a dead man. The poem reflects on human mortality, the limits of healing, the instability of happiness, and Hieron's illness while praising his prosperity and rule. It concludes that song preserves the fame of heroes such as Nestor and Sarpedon.

l: Hieron of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Hieron of Syracuse is praised as a king who rules his citizens benevolently and treats strangers like a father. The speaker wishes to bring him both golden health and a song celebrating Pherenikos's Pythian victory, and says that Destiny has favored him with happiness.

l: Pherenikos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Pherenikos is Hieron's horse, and he won the victory at Kirrha in the Pythian contest. His victory supplies the subject and splendour of Hieron's Pythian crown.

l: the Pythian victory of Pherenikos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The Pythian victory of Pherenikos was won at Kirrha and is celebrated in the ode. The speaker presents it as a source of joy and lasting glory for Hieron.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The ode is addressed to Hieron of Syracuse and celebrates Pherenikos's Pythian victory. It is concerned with Hieron's illness, the limits of mortal life, and the power of song to preserve virtue and fame.

l: Hieron's illness, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Hieron's illness occupies much of the ode's subject matter. The speaker wishes that golden health could accompany the song brought to Hieron.

l: Cheiron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Cheiron, the son of Philyra, is described as a humane and wise beast who once ruled in Pelion's glens. He trained Asklepios to devise remedies that save lives, and the speaker wishes that he were still alive so that he might provide a healer for worthy men.

l: Asklepios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Asklepios was trained by Cheiron as a healer and cured many bodily ailments through spells, potions, charms, and surgery. He was tempted by a great reward to restore a dead man to life, after which Zeus struck him down with lightning.

l: Koronis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Koronis, daughter of Phlegyas, conceived a child by Apollo but took another spouse, Ischys, without her father's knowledge. Apollo became aware of this, and Artemis killed Koronis before she could give birth.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Apollo fathered Koronis's unborn child and perceived her union with Ischys. Although he allowed her death, he rescued the child Asklepios from the burning funeral pyre and carried him to Cheiron for training.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Zeus is described as the father of Apollo and as one whose sons' wrath is not idle. He killed Asklepios and the man restored by him, striking them with lightning because Asklepios had brought a dead man back to life.

l: death, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Death claims Koronis before she can deliver her child and later takes Asklepios after Zeus strikes him down. The ode treats death as a boundary that even healing wisdom must not violate.

l: immortality, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The speaker advises his soul not to desire an immortal life. Mortal beings are urged instead to use the means and abilities available to them.

l: human mortality, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Human mortality is presented as an unavoidable condition, marked by illness, death, and the changing fortunes of life. The ode teaches that mortals should recognize the limits of their allotted path rather than seek what belongs to the gods.

l: Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Syracuse is the home of Hieron, the speaker's Aitnaian friend and king. The speaker imagines sailing to its fountain of Arethusa to bring Hieron health and a song of victory.

l: human destiny, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Destiny is said to have looked favorably upon Hieron, who is a chief and leader of a people. Yet destiny does not guarantee uninterrupted happiness, since even great figures endure suffering.

l: happiness, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Happiness is portrayed as unstable and short-lived when it comes in excessive measure. Peleus and Kadmos experienced great happiness but also later suffered bitter anguish, while Hieron is nevertheless said to possess an especially favorable lot.

l: Pytho, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Pytho is the place where Pherenikos won the race celebrated by the ode. Apollo is also said to have been at sheep-gathering in Pytho when he became aware of Koronis's unfaithfulness.

l: healing arts, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Healing is associated with Asklepios, who treated sores, wounds, and ailments through medicines, spells, charms, and surgery. The speaker wishes that Cheiron were alive to provide a healer for Hieron's illness, while the story warns that healing cannot rightly overcome death.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The ode celebrates Arkesilas of Kyrene's victory in the chariot-race and connects his lineage with the founding and colonization of Kyrene in Libya. It recounts Medea's prophecy, the Argonaut expedition led by Jason, the dispute between Jason and Pelias over the kingship of Iolkos, and Jason's quest for the Golden Fleece with Medea's aid. The poem traces the descent of Euphemos's line from the Argonauts to Battos and ultimately to Arkesilas. It also urges Arkesilas to restore Kyrene's political order and praises the exiled Demophilos for his wisdom and loyalty.

l: Arkesilas of Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Arkesilas is king of Kyrene and the victor in the chariot-race at Pytho. He is described as being in the eighth generation after Battos, and the ode praises his lineage while urging him to secure Kyrene's good destiny.

l: Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Kyrene is a city in Libya founded through the line descended from Euphemos and Battos. Its royal house is connected with Apollo, Pytho, and the Argonauts, and Arkesilas is urged to restore and govern it well.

l: Demophilos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Demophilos is associated with Kyrene's political troubles and is praised as a wise and righteous man who is temporarily exiled. He is said to be young in age but old in counsel, to reject insolence, and to hope to return home and live peacefully among citizens who value him.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Apollo is present at the oracle concerning Battos and Kyrene and later gives glory to Arkesilas in the chariot-race. He is also said to have given the descendants of Euphemos the Libyan plain and to have directed their settlement.

l: Battos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Battos is chosen by the Delphian oracle to found a power in fruitful Libya and to establish the city of Kyrene. He is identified as the ancestor whose eighth-generation descendant is Arkesilas.

l: Libya, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Libya is the continent destined to receive descendants of the Argonaut Euphemos. Its fertile plain is granted by Apollo to the line that settles Kyrene and honors the gods there.

l: Thera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Thera is the holy island from which Battos is instructed to depart in order to found Kyrene. Medea's prophecy declares Thera to be the mother-city of mighty communities.

l: Medea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Medea, daughter of Aietes and queen of the Colchians, prophesies the future colonization of Libya from Thera through Euphemos's line. During the Argonaut expedition she gives Jason magical protection and guidance, helps him complete Aietes's tasks, and flees with him after he takes the Fleece.

l: Aietes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Aietes is Medea's father and king in whose presence Jason and the Argonauts fight the Colchians. He sets Jason the tasks of ploughing with fire-breathing bulls and winning the Golden Fleece, but Jason completes them through Medea's aid.

l: Jason, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Jason returns to Iolkos to reclaim the kingship that Pelias has unlawfully taken from his family. He leads the Argonaut expedition, completes Aietes's dangerous tasks with Medea's help, obtains the Golden Fleece, and escapes with Medea after overcoming the dragon.

l: Argonauts, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The Argonauts are the godlike heroes who sail with Jason in search of the Golden Fleece. They receive Medea's prophecy, pass through dangerous regions, fight the Colchians, and return after the Fleece is taken.

l: Euphemos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Euphemos is an Argonaut who receives a clod of earth from the god Eurypylos, though it is accidentally lost into the sea. His descendants eventually settle in Kalliste and become the founders of the line that rules Kyrene.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Zeus confirms the significance of the earth clod given to Euphemos with a peal of thunder. Jason also invokes Zeus before the Argonauts begin their voyage, and thunder and lightning answer as favorable signs.

l: Poseidon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Poseidon is invoked as the lord of the sea during the Argonauts' voyage. The Argonauts establish a shrine and sacred precinct for him near the mouth of the Axine sea.

l: Pelias, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Pelias is warned by prophecy to fear a man wearing one sandal and is alarmed when Jason appears with that sign. He has unlawfully taken the kingship from Jason's family, then sends Jason to recover the Golden Fleece while promising to surrender the throne.

l: Iolkos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Iolkos is the glorious land and kingdom to which Jason returns after being raised by Cheiron. Its kingship is disputed because Pelias rules the throne that Jason claims as his ancestral right.

l: Cheiron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Cheiron raises Jason for twenty years in his cave, together with his daughters Chariklo and Philyra. Jason says that he learned wisdom from Cheiron and returns to Iolkos only after completing his upbringing.

l: Phrixos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Phrixos is said to demand that his ghost be laid to rest by the recovery of the Golden Fleece. His sacrifice and deliverance on the ram provide the reason Pelias gives for sending Jason on the expedition.

l: Kyrene's founding and colonization, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Kyrene's founding is foretold by Medea and confirmed by the Delphian oracle's choice of Battos. The city is ultimately colonized in Libya by descendants of Euphemos who come through Thera and Kalliste.

l: Arkesilas's chariot victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Arkesilas wins glory in the chariot-race at Pytho from the hands of the Amphiktyons. The ode is composed to celebrate this victory and to connect it with the divine and ancestral history of Kyrene.

l: oracle of God, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The Delphian oracle calls Battos three times and declares him destined to be king of Kyrene. The oracle at Pytho also directs a later descendant to lead ships toward the rich Nile region.

l: Argonaut expedition, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The Argonaut expedition begins when Jason gathers heroes at Iolkos to seek the Golden Fleece and fulfill the mission associated with Phrixos. The company sails under favorable omens, reaches Colchis, fights Aietes's forces, and departs with Medea and the Fleece.

l: Argo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Argo is the ship that carries Jason and the Argonauts on their dangerous voyage. The heroes anchor her during their travels and later sail her to the Phasis in Colchis.

l: Golden Fleece, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The Golden Fleece is the imperishable golden covering of the ram that carried Phrixos to safety. Pelias sends Jason to recover it, but it is guarded in a thick wood by a huge dragon until Jason takes it with Medea's assistance.

l: Medea's prophecy, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Medea prophesies that descendants of the Argonauts will establish cities in Libya and that Thera will become the mother-city of powerful communities. Her prophecy specifically links Euphemos's line with the later founding of Kyrene.

l: single sandal prophecy, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: An oracle warns Pelias to guard against the man who comes wearing one sandal. Jason fulfills the sign when he arrives in Iolkos with a single sandal on his right foot, causing Pelias to recognize the danger.

l: Pelias's kingship dispute with Jason, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Jason claims the throne of his ancestors because Pelias has unlawfully taken it from his family. Jason offers Pelias the herds and lands but demands the ancestral scepter and throne, while Pelias proposes the quest for the Golden Fleece as the condition for surrendering rule.

l: Medea's aid to Jason, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Medea gives Jason drugs mixed with oil that protect him from the fire and power of Aietes's bulls. She teaches him prayers and charms, helps him complete the appointed tasks, and assists him in taking the Golden Fleece and escaping.

l: dragon guarding the Golden Fleece, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The Golden Fleece lies in a thick wood under the guard of a huge, glaring, speckled dragon. Jason kills or overcomes the dragon through subtlety with Medea's help and then takes the Fleece.

l: Kyrene's political restoration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The ode urges Arkesilas to act as a timely physician and set Kyrene firmly in its place. It presents the restoration of a troubled city as difficult but possible when God guides the ruler's hand, and associates Demophilos with the wise counsel needed for that work.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, [Footnote 1: Libya. Epaphos was son of Zeus by Io.]
s: Libya is connected with Epaphos, who was the son of Zeus and Io, and with a future colony founded by Battos. Euphemos was told that his descendants would first colonize Thera and, after seventeen generations, found Kyrene in Libya. Thera was identified as the island where a clod dropped by Euphemos would wash ashore. Kyrene is identified with the city whose fountain was called Kyra.

l: Libya, The Extant Odes of Pindar, [Footnote 1: Libya. Epaphos was son of Zeus by Io.]
s: Libya is associated with Epaphos, the son of Zeus and Io. It was to receive a colony founded by Battos after Euphemos’ descendants had first colonized Thera.

l: Thera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, [Footnote 1: Libya. Epaphos was son of Zeus by Io.]
s: Thera was the island where the clod dropped by Euphemos into the sea was expected to wash ashore. Euphemos’ descendants were to colonize Thera before proceeding, after seventeen generations, to found Kyrene in Libya.

l: Euphemos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, [Footnote 1: Libya. Epaphos was son of Zeus by Io.]
s: Euphemos dropped a clod into the sea instead of carrying it safely home to Tainaros. Because of this, his descendants were destined to colonize Thera first and later found Kyrene in Libya.

l: Battos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, [Footnote 1: Libya. Epaphos was son of Zeus by Io.]
s: Battos was to lead the later foundation of Kyrene in Libya, after Euphemos’ descendants had colonized Thera and seventeen generations had passed.

l: Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, [Footnote 1: Libya. Epaphos was son of Zeus by Io.]
s: Kyrene was to be founded in Libya by Battos after the intervening colonization of Thera. The fountain Kyra was located in the heart of the city Kyrene.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Ode V celebrates Arkesilas of Kyrene's victory in the chariot-race at the Pythian games. Karrhotos, Arkesilas's wife's brother, drove the chariot safely through twelve turns and returned with the honor of victory, while the chariot's equipment was dedicated at Delphi. The ode praises Arkesilas's wealth, kingship, divine favor, and lineage from Battos, and recounts Apollo's role in the foundation and protection of Kyrene. It also describes the sacred procession along Apollo's street and prays that Zeus will preserve Arkesilas's prosperity and grant the seed of Battos comparable renown at Olympia.

l: Arkesilas of Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Arkesilas is celebrated as the winner of the chariot-race at the Pythian games. He is praised as a divinely favored king of mighty cities, wealthy, righteous, wise beyond his years, eloquent, courageous, and gifted with the Muses. The ode prays that he will retain divine favor and that his descendants will win similar renown at Olympia.

l: Karrhotos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Karrhotos, the brother of Arkesilas's wife, drove Arkesilas's chariot at the Pythian games. He handled the reins safely through twelve swift turns without breaking the strong harness and returned crowned with victory. Arkesilas is urged to honor him as his chief friend.

l: Battos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Battos is remembered as the founder and ancestral ruler of Kyrene. His ancient good fortune is said to continue with his race, and his city is protected by his legacy. Apollo caused lions to flee when Battos spoke to them in a foreign accent, fulfilling Apollo's oracle concerning Kyrene.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Apollo is presented as the captain and founder of Kyrene, the source of its oracles, and the god who protected Battos and caused the lions to flee. He gives cures for illnesses, the lute, and the Muse, and established the Herakleidai and Aigimios's descendants in several places. His sacred street and temple are associated with the procession and the dedication of Arkesilas's chariot equipment.

l: Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Kyrene is Arkesilas's city and the destination of the victorious horses and their charioteer. Its people sing Arkesilas's praise around Aphrodite's garden and honor Apollo's Karneia. Kyrene was founded by Battos, and its sacred street, groves, market-place, tombs, and heroic traditions are described.

l: Delphi, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Delphi is the place where the chariot was apparently consecrated to Apollo and left in the temple. Karrhotos won the victory beside the waters of Kastalia, and the chariot's equipment was hung in a cypress-wood chamber near a statue in the Parnassian shrine.

l: Pythian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The Pythian games granted Arkesilas glory through his horses and supplied the subject of the triumphal song. At the games, Karrhotos won the chariot-race and received a crown beside the waters of Kastalia.

l: Arkesilas's chariot victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The victory was won by Arkesilas's team at the Pythian games, with Karrhotos driving. Among forty charioteers who fell, Karrhotos brought his chariot through unhurt and completed the twelve turns safely.

l: Kyrene's founding and colonization, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The foundation of Kyrene is attributed to Battos, also called Aristoteles, whom Apollo guided and whose settlers reached the city by sea. Battos planted groves for the gods, made a paved sacred road across the plain, and was worshipped as a hero after his death.

l: sacred procession of Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The victorious horses were brought home to Kyrene and led in procession through Apollo's sacred street. The procession moved along the paved road while songs sought Apollo's guardianship for the people.

l: Ode V, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Ode V celebrates the same chariot victory as the preceding ode. It praises Arkesilas, Karrhotos, Apollo, Battos, and the history and sacred traditions of Kyrene.

l: chariot, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The chariot associated with Arkesilas's victory was apparently consecrated to Apollo and left at Delphi. Its harness and other workmanship were hung in Apollo's temple near a natural wooden statue in the Parnassian shrine.

l: horses, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Arkesilas won glory at the Pythian games through his horses. They were brought back to Kyrene and led in procession through Apollo's sacred street.

l: sacred street of Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The sacred street of Apollo was a paved road cut straight across the plain for processions seeking Apollo's protection. The victorious horses were led along it through Kyrene, and Battos was buried apart at its end near the market-place.

l: wealth, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Wealth is described as powerful when Fate gives it to a mortal together with pure virtue. Arkesilas possesses great wealth and is praised for using prosperity righteously and wisely.

l: divine favor, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Arkesilas's success, prosperity, and strength are attributed to divine favor. The ode asks the children of Kronos to preserve his favor in Arkesilas's counsel and actions and to grant lasting renown to Battos's descendants.

l: Destiny, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The ode says that no one has ever been entirely free from trouble, and that fortune varies. Nevertheless, Battos's ancient bliss continues to protect his race and city, while the destiny of those loved by Zeus is guided by Zeus's mighty mind.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The unit celebrates Xenokrates of Akragas as winner of the chariot-race victory won in B.C. 494 and presents the ode as a treasure of song for Xenokrates, the Emmenidai, and Akragas. It praises the victory at Krisa and links Xenokrates with the honor owed to parents, especially through the examples of Achilles and Antilochos. Antilochos is remembered for dying to save his father Nestor from Memnon, while Thrasyboulos is praised for wisdom, generosity, and honorable use of wealth. The poem also invokes Apollo's sanctuary at Delphi and Poseidon, the Earthshaker who devised ventures of steeds.

l: Xenokrates of Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Xenokrates is honored as the winner of the chariot-race victory celebrated in the ode. A ready treasure of song is built for him in Apollo's valley, and the poem praises his observance of parental honor and his connection with Thrasyboulos.

l: Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Akragas is described as a riverside city for which the treasure of song is built, together with the Emmenidai and Xenokrates.

l: chariot-race victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The victory was won in B.C. 494 and was achieved at the chariot-race. Its glory was won in the dells of Krisa and is presented as enduring through song.

l: chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The chariot-race is the contest in which Xenokrates won the victory celebrated by the ode.

l: the Emmenidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The Emmenidai are among those for whom a lasting treasure of song is built in Apollo's valley.

l: Delphi, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The ode was probably intended to be sung at Delphi immediately after the victory.

l: song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Song is portrayed as a treasure built for Xenokrates, the Emmenidai, and Akragas. Its clear light will announce the victory, and neither wind nor winter storm will carry it away into the sea.

l: Thrasyboulos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Thrasyboulos is addressed as Xenokrates's father in the poem and receives the glory of the victory along with his kin. He is praised for following his uncle, handling wealth wisely, avoiding unrighteous and overweening youth, welcoming guests, and cultivating knowledge among the Pierides.

l: Antilochos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Antilochos is remembered as a mighty man who died for his father when he faced the murderous attack of Memnon. He was judged supreme among the young men of ancient times in succoring parents.

l: Memnon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Memnon is identified as the leader of the Ethiopian hosts. He attacked Nestor with his mighty spear while Nestor's chariot was stopped by a horse wounded by Paris's arrows.

l: Antilochos's death for his father, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Antilochos died while taking his father's place against Memnon, thereby buying Nestor's escape. His sacrifice was regarded as a mighty deed and as the supreme example of helping one's parents.

l: parental honor and duty, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Parental honor requires reverence for Kronos's son above all gods and forbids robbing a parent of the honor due to a lifetime. The poem illustrates this duty through Achilles' instruction and Antilochos's sacrifice for Nestor.

l: horses and chariots, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The poem celebrates ventures of steeds devised by the Earthshaker. In the story of Antilochos, Nestor's chariot is stopped when one of its horses is struck by Paris's arrows, leaving Antilochos to defend his father.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: The unit celebrates Megakles of Athens, winner of the four-horse chariot-race in B.C. 490, the year of the battle of Marathon. Megakles belonged to the great house of the Alkmaionidai and was probably the nephew, or possibly the son, of Kleisthenes. The poem praises Athens and the Alkmaionidai, recalls victories won by Megakles and his father at Isthmos, Olympia, and Kirrha, and acknowledges the envy that accompanied Megakles's success. Megakles was twice ostracized.

l: Megakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Megakles of Athens won the four-horse chariot-race in B.C. 490. He belonged to the Alkmaionidai and was probably the nephew, or possibly the son, of Kleisthenes. He and his father had won victories at Isthmos, Olympia, and Kirrha, and he was twice ostracized.

l: Athens, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Athens is praised as the fairest and most glorious name with which to begin songs celebrating the Alkmaionidai and their horses. Its citizens are identified with Erechtheus and are associated with the building of a glorious house for Apollo at divine Pytho.

l: four-horse chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: The four-horse chariot-race was won by Megakles of Athens in B.C. 490, the year of the battle of Marathon.

l: Megakles's victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Megakles's victory in the four-horse chariot-race is celebrated alongside victories won by Megakles and his father at Isthmos, Olympia, and Kirrha. The poem rejoices in this new good fortune but also grieves that envy requites noble deeds.

l: Alkmaionidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: The Alkmaionidai were a great house to which Kleisthenes and Perikles belonged. Megakles was a member of the family, and the poem presents Athens and its fame as a foundation for songs about the Alkmaionidai and their horses.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: The ode celebrates Aristomenes of Aigina as winner of the wrestling-match at the Pythian games and praises his athletic successes at several other contests. It invokes Peace and Righteousness, praises Aigina and the deeds of the sons of Aiakos, and credits Apollo with granting Aristomenes his victory. The poem also recalls Amphiaraos, Alkmaion, and the prophetic story of the Epigonoi before praying for the continued prosperity of Xenarches and his family. It ends by asking Aigina, with Zeus, Aiakos, Peleus, Telamon, and Achilles, to guard the city.

l: Aristomenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Aristomenes wins the wrestling-match at the Pythian games. He has also won at Megara, Marathon, and the games of Hera in Aigina, and is praised as the youngest of his country's glories and as a member of the clan of the Midylidai.

l: Xenarches, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Xenarches is the father of Aristomenes. Apollo is said to have welcomed him home from Kirrha, and the poet prays that divine favour may remain with his fortune and that of his family.

l: Peace, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Peace is called the daughter of Righteousness and the power that makes cities great. She holds the supreme keys of counsels and wars, gives and receives gentleness, and sinks Insolence in the sea when moved to wrath.

l: Righteousness, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Righteousness is presented as the mother of Peace and as a force associated with the order of the ode. She stands beside the song of triumph, and the poet prays for God's favour toward Xenarches and his family.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Aigina is praised as a righteous island-commonwealth famed for the deeds of the sons of Aiakos. She is described as a nurse of heroes and as pre-eminent in games and violent fights, and the poet asks her to guard the city.

l: Pythian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: The Pythian games award Aristomenes the victory in the wrestling-match. The Pythian feast grants him the glad return and welcomes him to his mother's side, while his defeated competitors lack that joy.

l: wrestling-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: The wrestling-match is won by Aristomenes at the Pythian games. He overcomes four other competitors in it.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Apollo brings down Typhon and the king of giants by the thunderbolt and the bow. He welcomes Xenarches home from Kirrha and grants Aristomenes the greatest joy of victory at Pytho.

l: Aiakids, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: The sons of Aiakos are credited with glorious deeds that contribute to Aigina's fame. Aristomenes is said to be following their example through his athletic achievements.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Aiakos is named among the heroic protectors associated with Aigina. The final prayer asks Aigina, together with Zeus and Aiakos, to guard the city.

l: Amphiaraos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Amphiaraos speaks prophetically during the story of the second enterprise against Thebes. He recognizes the noble nature of Alkmaion, foresees better tidings for Adrastos, and predicts that Adrastos alone of the Danaans will return safely with his people.

l: Alkmaion, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Alkmaion is identified by Amphiaraos as carrying a speckled dragon on his shield and standing foremost at the Kadmean gates. The poet throws garlands and songs upon Alkmaion's grave, describing him as a neighbour and guardian of his possessions and as the source of a prophetic sign at the earth's centre-stone.

l: Delphi, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: The poet is associated with a journey to Delphi, described in the note as a journey to the earth's centre-stone. At that place Alkmaion showed forth the prophetic gift belonging to his house.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Zeus is named with Aiakos, Peleus, Telamon, and Achilles in the final prayer for the protection of Aigina and its city.

l: Achilles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Achilles is named as one of the heroic figures associated with Aigina and the line of Aiakos. The poet asks Aigina to guard the city together with him and the other named heroes.

l: victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Aristomenes' victory is won in the wrestling-match at the Pythian games and is presented as a divinely granted joy. His other victories include contests at Megara, Marathon, and the games of Hera in Aigina.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The unit celebrates Telesikrates of Kyrene, winner of the foot-race in full armour at Pytho, and praises the honour he brought to Kyrene. It recounts how Apollo carried the huntress-maiden Kyrene from Pelion to Libya, where she became queen and joined with Apollo, and how their son Aristaios was established as a benefactor of flocks and agriculture. It also links Telesikrates and Kyrene with Thebes, Herakles, and earlier contests, especially through praise of heroic deeds and timely action. The closing story compares Telesikrates’s victory with Alexidamos’s winning of the daughter of Antaios through a foot-race arranged as a marriage contest.

l: Telesikrates, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Telesikrates, son of Karneadas, won the foot-race in full armour at Pytho and brought honour to Kyrene. His victory was celebrated as a sign of good fortune, and the maidens of Kyrene and elsewhere wished for such a man as a husband or son.

l: Kyrene (the huntress-maiden), The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Kyrene was a strong huntress who disliked weaving and household feasts, fought wild beasts with spear and sword, and protected her father’s herds. Apollo found her wrestling a lion, and she became his bride and queen in Libya.

l: Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Kyrene is praised as a city of charioteers that received glory through Telesikrates’s victory. It is also described as the city founded through the destiny of the huntress-maiden Kyrene.

l: Pytho, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Pytho was the place where Telesikrates won the foot-race in full armour. The victory there proclaimed the name of Kyrene and joined the city’s fame to Delphi.

l: the foot-race in full armour, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The foot-race in full armour had been instituted at Pytho for the kind of rapid advance required of a Hellenic heavy-armed soldier. Telesikrates won it in 478.

l: victory at Pytho, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The victory at Pytho gave Telesikrates glory and proclaimed Kyrene’s name. It is treated as a fortunate achievement worthy of public song.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Apollo, called the far-darting son of Leto, carried Kyrene from Pelion in a golden car and made her queen in Libya. He found her fighting a lion, desired her as his bride, and joined with her in a golden chamber.

l: Cheiron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Cheiron was summoned by Apollo to witness Kyrene’s struggle with the lion and to explain her lineage. He foretold that Apollo would take her to Libya, where she would become queen and bear a son.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Zeus is associated with the chosen garden and broad meadow-lands of Libya where Apollo would establish Kyrene. Aristaios is described as being made like an immortal, a Zeus or a holy Apollo, through the care of the divine powers.

l: Libya, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Libya, described as a land of broad meadow-lands and rich produce, received Kyrene as Apollo’s bride. It gave her a portion of land and became the place where she bore their son.

l: the city of Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The city of Kyrene is portrayed as the beautiful city associated with the huntress-maiden who became its queen and namesake. Telesikrates’s victory caused its name to be proclaimed and brought it precious honour.

l: Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Seven-gated Thebes is connected with Kyrene through the Aigid family and is invoked as a place that remembers Iolaos’s timely deed. It also nurtured Herakles and Iphikles through the waters of Dirke.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Herakles is praised as a figure whom no one should fail to celebrate. The speaker credits Herakles and Iphikles, together with the waters of Dirke that nurtured them, in connection with his own successful song.

l: the daughter of Antaios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The daughter of Antaios was a renowned Libyan maiden whose beauty attracted both kinsmen and foreign suitors. Her father arranged a race in which the first man to touch her robes would take her as his bride.

l: Alexidamos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Alexidamos won the race arranged for the daughter of Antaios by reaching her first and taking her hand. He led her away through the Nomad horsemen and was showered with leaves and wreaths.

l: the wedding of the Libyan princess, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The wedding of the Libyan princess was determined by a foot-race, with the maiden herself standing at the finish as the prize. Alexidamos won and led her away as his bride.

l: the bridal union of Apollo and Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The bridal union of Apollo and Kyrene took place quickly in a golden chamber of Libya after Apollo and Cheiron discussed her destiny. Their union made Kyrene queen and produced a son whom Hermes carried to the Hours and Earth.

l: Kyrene's founding and colonization, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The founding of Kyrene is presented as the fulfillment of Apollo’s taking Kyrene from Pelion to Libya and establishing her as queen. The city became associated with her name, beauty, flocks, produce, and games.

l: Pythian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The Pythian games provided the setting for Telesikrates’s victory in the foot-race in full armour. His success there was celebrated as a public honour for Kyrene.

l: the praise of Kyrene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The praise of Kyrene is voiced through celebration of Telesikrates’s victory, the city’s fame, and the story of its divine and heroic origins. The speaker says that he has already sung Kyrene’s praise at Aigma and on the hill of Nisos.

l: poetry and song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Poetry and song are presented as means of proclaiming victory, honouring noble deeds, and preserving ancient glory. The speaker values brevity suited to the occasion and asks that the voice of the Graces not abandon him.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The ode celebrates Hippokleas of Thessaly, winner of the two-stadion foot-race of boys at Pytho. Pindar praises Hippokleas, his father, his host Thorax, and the Aleuadai, while linking Thessaly and Lakedaimon to Herakles and Perseus. A long digression describes Perseus's visit to the Hyperborean folk and his slaying of the Gorgon. The unit is identified as Pindar's earliest surviving complete poem, written when he was twenty years old.

l: Hippokleas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Hippokleas is celebrated as the winner of the two-stadion foot-race of boys at Pytho. His victory is praised among the people around Parnassos, and Pindar hopes to make him more glorious through song and cause him to be admired by young maidens and by his peers and elders.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Pindar composed the ode for Hippokleas, at the request of Thorax. He praises Hippokleas, his family, and Thessaly, and the text identifies this as the earliest entire surviving poem by Pindar, written when he was twenty years old.

l: Thorax, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Thorax engaged Pindar to write the ode for Hippokleas and is described as Pindar's host. Pindar trusts in Thorax's kindly courtesy and compares him to a friend and willing guide who has yoked the four-horse car of the Pierides to advance Pindar's fortune.

l: Aleuadai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The Aleuadai are associated with Hippokleas and with the request for a chorus celebrating him. They are said to be descended through Herakles from Perseus, and Pindar praises Thorax and his noble brothers for strengthening the Thessalian commonwealth.

l: Perseus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Perseus is presented as an ancient chieftain who visited the Hyperborean folk while they sacrificed asses to Apollo. With Athene leading him, he also slew the Gorgon and carried home her serpent-haired head, which brought a stony death to the island folk.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Apollo is invoked as the source of Hippokleas's achievements and inborn excellence. He especially enjoys the feasts and hymns of the Hyperborean folk and laughs at the braying of their asses.

l: Lakedaimon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Lakedaimon is called happy and blessed. It is said to share with Thessaly a ruling race descended from Herakles, who is described as bravest in battle.

l: Thessaly, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Thessaly is called happy and blessed and is linked with Lakedaimon through a race descended from Herakles. Pindar hopes to make Hippokleas more glorious among the people of Ephyra by singing of his victories, and he praises Thorax and his brothers for exalting the Thessalians' commonwealth.

l: Pytho, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Pytho calls Pindar to celebrate Hippokleas. At Pytho, Hippokleas won the two-stadion foot-race of boys and received the Pythian crown.

l: the Hyperborean folk, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The Hyperborean folk are described as a blessed and hallowed people who live without pestilence, wasting old age, toil, or war. They feast and sing for Apollo, perform dances, play pipes, and crown themselves with golden bay leaves; Perseus once entered their homes while they sacrificed asses to Apollo.

l: two-stadion foot-race of boys, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The two-stadion foot-race of boys is the event that Hippokleas won. It is described as a race down the stadion and back, and his victory at Pytho made him foremost among the boys who ran it.

l: Pythian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The Pythian Games are associated with Hippokleas's crown at Pytho and with victories won beneath the cliff of Kirrha. The text also refers to a race in full armor at Pytho and to Hippokleas's father being twice victorious at Olympia in armor.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The ode celebrates Hippokleas's victory and praises his family, Thorax, the Aleuadai, Thessaly, and Lakedaimon. It contains a long account of Perseus and the Hyperborean folk, and it is described as Pindar's earliest surviving complete poem, written when he was twenty.

l: the Perseus digression, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The Perseus digression occupies much of the ode and recounts Perseus's visit to the Hyperborean folk and his slaying of the Gorgon. The text says that its apparent reason is that Thorax, and perhaps Hippokleas, belonged to the Aleuadai, who were descended through Herakles from Perseus.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The unit celebrates Thrasydaios of Thebes, winner of the boys' short foot-race at Kirrha in B.C. 478. His victory made his father's house glorious, adding a third wreath to its honors, while his father had previously won at Pytho. The ode invokes Theban and heroic figures, recounts the murder of Agamemnon and the vengeance of Orestes, and praises modest service to the common good. It also declares that the middle course is most enduring in the commonwealth and condemns tyranny.

l: Thrasydaios of Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Thrasydaios won the boys' short foot-race at Kirrha in the rich cornlands of Pylades. His victory made his father's house glorious by adding a third wreath, and his speed put the host of the Hellenes to shame.

l: Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Thebes is honored as the seven-gated city. Its daughters and heroic sisterhood are summoned to sing at the Ismenian shrine in praise of the city and Thrasydaios's victory.

l: boys' short foot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The boys' short foot-race was won by Thrasydaios at the games at Kirrha. His victory was among the honors that glorified his father's house.

l: Lakonian Orestes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Lakonian Orestes is named as the guest-hosted by Pylades in the account of the land associated with Thrasydaios's victory. After Agamemnon's murder, Orestes was saved by his nurse Arsinoë and became the guest of the old man Strophios at the foot of Parnassos; he later slew his mother and left Aigisthos's body in its blood.

l: Agamemnon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Agamemnon, son of Atreus, was murdered after returning from Troy, and Kassandra was killed with him by Klytaimnestra. The unit says that he died at famous Amyklai after consuming the Trojans' dwellings, though it notes that this is a strange variant of the tale.

l: commonwealth, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The speaker says that the middle course prospers most enduringly in the commonwealth. He devotes his efforts to well-doing for the common good and praises excellence carried with modesty rather than insolence.

l: tyranny, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The speaker condemns a state of tyranny. He presents it in opposition to the more enduring prosperity of the middle course in the commonwealth.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: This early ode celebrates Midas of Akragas, winner of a flute-playing match, whose victory was won either in 494 or 450. It welcomes Midas and his crown from Pytho to Akragas, where the poem is probably performed in procession to the city’s tutelar shrine. The ode attributes the invention of the flute to Athene, who created it to imitate the lament of the Gorgons after Perseus killed Medusa. It concludes that human success requires labor and that fate may grant unexpected blessings while withholding others.

l: Midas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Midas is celebrated as the winner of the flute-playing match and as having gained renown through a crown brought from Pytho. He is welcomed to Akragas after overcoming all Hellas in flute-playing.

l: Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Akragas is praised as a splendid and beautiful city, the haunt of Persephone, situated by a stream that nourishes flocks and crowned by a pleasant citadel. It is presented as the place where Midas and his victory crown are welcomed.

l: flute-playing match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The flute-playing match is the contest in which Midas overcame all Hellas. Its victory may have occurred in either 494 or 450.

l: victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The victory is Midas' success in the flute-playing match, commemorated by a crown that came from Pytho. The poem suggests that such human bliss and achievement are not made manifest without labor.

l: Athene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Athene devised the music of the flute after hearing the Gorgon's death-lament. She created the instrument so that the shrill lament reaching from Euryale's jaws could be repeated and gave the music to mortal men.

l: Gorgons, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The Gorgons are described as having maiden heads and unapproachable serpent heads, and their lament was heard during the anguish following Perseus' attack. Their death-lament became the model for Athene's flute music.

l: Perseus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Perseus struck down Medusa, the third sister, and carried her doom to Seriphos and its people. He also blinded the wondrous brood of Phorkos and brought Medusa's head as a grievous gift to Polydektes' bridal.

l: Gorgon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Medusa is identified as the fair-faced third sister of the Gorgons and the daughter of Danaë, said to have sprung from a living stream of gold. Perseus won her head after striking her down.

l: the flute, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The flute was devised by Athene as a means of repeating the Gorgons' shrill lament. Its music is described as a many-headed air produced through thin-beat bronze and reeds, and it became a possession of mortal men.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, THE NEMEAN ODES.
s: The unit consists solely of the title “THE NEMEAN ODES.” It concerns a work identified as The Nemean Odes. No further information is provided about its contents, subjects, or events.

l: The Nemean Odes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, THE NEMEAN ODES.
s: The Nemean Odes is identified as the title of the unit. No additional information about it is provided.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Nemean Ode I celebrates Chromios of Aitna, winner of the chariot-race at Nemea, and is presented as a song performed before his house in Ortygia. It praises Aitna, Syracuse, Sicily, Zeus, and Chromios’s generosity and abilities. Much of the ode recounts Herakles’ childhood victory over the serpents sent by Hera and Teiresias’s prophecy of Herakles’ future labors, battle against the giants, rest among the immortals, and marriage to Hebe.

l: Nemean Ode I, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Nemean Ode I is addressed to Chromios of Aitna, winner in the chariot-race. It praises his victory, Aitna, Syracuse, and the gods, and includes the story and prophecy of Herakles.

l: Chromios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Chromios is praised as the victor whose car and victory at Nemea inspire the triumphal song. He is called the son of Agesidamos and is presented as possessing both practical ability and foresight, as well as generosity toward friends and strangers.

l: Ortygia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Ortygia is called the august resting-place of Alpheos, a scion of Syracuse, a couch of Artemis, and a sister of Delos. From Ortygia the song goes forth, apparently before the house of Chromios.

l: Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Syracuse is identified as the famous source from which Ortygia springs. The ode also calls for splendid words in honor of the isle associated with Syracuse.

l: Aitna, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Aitna is honored through Chromios’s victory and through the praise of Aitnaian Zeus. Chromios is identified as a man of Aitna.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Zeus is called Aitnaian and lord of Olympus. He gave the isle of Sicily to Persephone, and Zeus’s son is said to have foretold Herakles’ divine reward and dwelling among the immortals.

l: Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Nemea and Chromios’s car stir the speaker to compose a triumphal song for Chromios’s victorious deeds.

l: Sicily, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Sicily is described as a teeming land that Zeus gave to Persephone and intended to exalt as the best land in the fruitful earth, crowned with citadels.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Herakles is celebrated for his ancient deeds of valor. As an infant he strangled two serpents sent against him, and Teiresias prophesied that he would destroy many monsters, defeat enemies, fight beside the gods against the giants, receive rest from his labors, and marry Hebe.

l: Hera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Hera is angered when Herakles and his twin-brother come into the light. In her anger she sends two serpents to attack the children.

l: Alkmene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Alkmene is startled from her couch when the serpents attack the children. She tries to beat back the violence of the fierce beasts.

l: serpents sent by Hera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: The two serpents sent by Hera enter the children’s bedchamber to entwine the children and make them prey to their teeth. Herakles seizes them by the necks and strangles them.

l: Amphitryon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Amphitryon comes running with a drawn sword after the serpents attack the children. He is first struck with pain and fear, but then feels gladness when he sees Herakles’ extraordinary courage and strength.

l: Teiresias, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Teiresias, described as a chosen prophet and true seer of Zeus, is summoned by Amphitryon. He prophesies Herakles’ destruction of monsters and insolent enemies, his role in the battle at Phlegra, his eternal rest among the immortals, and his marriage to Hebe.

l: giants, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: The giants are destined to meet the gods in battle on the plain of Phlegra. Teiresias foretells that their bright hair will be soiled with earth beneath the rush of Herakles’ arrows.

l: gods, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: The gods are prophesied to meet the giants in battle at Phlegra. Herakles is foretold to fight with them and afterward receive a reward of rest.

l: Hebe, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Hebe is foretold to become Herakles’ bride. After receiving her, Herakles will hold a marriage feast and remain beside Zeus in the divine dwelling.

l: chariot-race victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: The chariot-race victory belongs to Chromios of Aitna. It is the occasion for the triumphal song and for the ode’s praise of Chromios.

l: Chromios’s car, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Chromios’s car, together with Nemea, inspires the speaker to yoke a melody of triumph to Chromios’s deeds.

l: Phlegra, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Phlegra’s plain is named as the place where the gods and giants will meet in battle. Herakles is prophesied to soil the giants’ bright hair with earth there.

l: battle of the gods and giants, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: The battle of the gods and giants is prophesied to take place on Phlegra’s plain. Herakles will aid the gods with his arrows and overcome the giants.

l: Herakles’ labors, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: Herakles’ labors include destroying lawless monsters on land and sea and delivering hateful, deceitful, insolent men to death. After these great toils, he is prophesied to receive a lasting reward of rest among the immortals.

l: prophecy of Teiresias, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode I
s: The prophecy of Teiresias describes Herakles’ future destruction of monsters and enemies, his participation in the battle against the giants at Phlegra, and his reward of eternal rest. It also foretells Herakles’ marriage to Hebe and his dwelling beside Zeus.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The note explains the phrase “so honoured by Artemis.” It indicates that the subject receives enough honor from Artemis to rank with her native Delos. The comparison establishes Delos as a place especially associated with Artemis.

l: Artemis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Artemis is described as honoring an unspecified subject to such a degree that it ranks with her native Delos.

l: Delos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Delos is identified as native to Artemis and serves as the standard of comparison for the honor granted to an unspecified subject.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: The ode celebrates Timodemos of Athens, who won the pankration at Nemea. It predicts that he will win further victories at the Isthmian and Pythian games. Timodemos is praised as a worthy descendant of the Timodemidai of Salamis and Acharnai, whose family had already gained many athletic crowns. The citizens are urged to welcome him home and sing a victory song in his honor.

l: Timodemos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: Timodemos of Athens won the pankration at Nemea. He is identified as the son of Timonoös and is praised for his stubborn prowess; the ode predicts that he will win again at the Isthmian and Pythian games.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: Nemeaian Zeus is invoked as the deity whose grove witnessed Timodemos laying the foundation of his victory. The citizens are also told to celebrate him at the games of Zeus.

l: Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: Nemea is described as the famous grove of Nemeaian Zeus, where Timodemos gained his first foundation of victory in the sacred games.

l: Athens, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: Athens is glorified through Timodemos, who is described as a glory of the city.

l: Salamis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: Salamis is said to be well able to rear a man of battles. Its association with Timodemos is compared with Salamis's Aias at Troy.

l: Timodemidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: The Timodemidai are associated with Acharnai and rank there pre-eminent in games. They won four victories beneath Parnassos, eight crowns in the valleys of Pelops at Corinth, and seven at Nemea, besides many victories at home.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: The pankration is the contest in which Timodemos won at Nemea. His success is attributed to his stubborn prowess in the event.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: The ode predicts that Timodemos will repeatedly win the noble flower of the Isthmian games.

l: Pythian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: The ode predicts that Timodemos will conquer in the Pythian games.

l: Nemean Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: The Timodemidai had obtained seven crowns at Nemea. Timodemos also established his first foundation of victory in the sacred games there.

l: victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode II
s: Timodemos's victory at Nemea is presented as the beginning of further expected victories. The ode celebrates victory through a song of triumph and calls for his honorable return home.
